Ẹ̀wờ̀ - Taboos & Assertions

Runtime constraints inspired by Yoruba spiritual prohibitions

Ewo implementation is partial

The parser handles ewo / assert / taboo statements, and the compiler compiles the condition expression. However, no runtime assertion opcode exists yet — the condition is evaluated but not enforced at the bytecode level.

What is Ewo?

Ẹ̀wờ̀ (Yoruba: "taboo/prohibition") defines runtime constraints that must be satisfied. If an Ẹ̀wờ̀ is violated, the program panics with a clear error message. Think of them as spiritual guardrails for your code.

Taboo Violations = Program Panic

Unlike soft assertions, Ewo violations are fatal. Use them for invariants that must NEVER be broken.

Basic Syntax

ewo condition;

Assert that a condition is true. Panics if false.

// Simple assertion
ayanmo age = 25;
ewo age >= 0;  // OK

ayanmo balance = -100;
ewo balance >= 0;  // PANIC: Taboo violated!

ewo condition, "message";

Assert with a custom error message.

ayanmo users = [];
ewo Ogunda.iwờn(users) > 0, "User list cannot be empty";

// If empty: PANIC: Taboo violated: User list cannot be empty

English Alias

assert condition, "message";

English alias for ewo.

// Both are equivalent:
ewo x > 0, "x must be positive";
assert x > 0, "x must be positive";

Common Patterns

Preconditions

Check inputs at function start.

fn divide(a, b) {
    ewo b != 0, "Division by zero forbidden";
    pada a / b;
}

Postconditions

Verify results before returning.

fn sqrt(n) {
    ewo n >= 0, "Cannot sqrt negative";
    ayanmo result = Obara.gbongbo(n);
    ewo result >= 0, "sqrt must be non-negative";
    pada result;
}

Loop Invariants

Ensure conditions hold during iteration.

ayanmo i = 0;
nigba (i < 100) {
    ewo i >= 0, "Loop counter went negative!";
    // ... loop body
    i = i + 1;
}

Type Guards

Validate data types at runtime.

fn process(data) {
    ewo Ogunda.iwờn(data) <= 1000, "List too large";
    // ... process data
}

Ewo vs Error Handling

Use Case Mechanism
Invariants that must never break ewo
Expected failures (file not found) Okanran.kigbe()
User input validation ti / bibẹkờ (if/else)
Bug detection in development ewo

Cultural Context

In Yoruba tradition, Ẹ̀wờ̀ are sacred prohibitions — things that must never be done. Breaking an Ẹ̀wờ̀ brings spiritual consequences. In Ifá-Lang, breaking an Ẹ̀wờ̀ brings program termination. Both serve the same purpose: enforcing boundaries that maintain harmony and correctness.
